events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Theo proposes Theo, Priya. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good and can trust myself on the mission. I will pair myself with Priya to start gathering information on Mission 1.

I support this team. Let me share what I know and what I don't.

I am a Loyal Servant. That means I know with certainty that I am Good, and I know nothing about anyone else's hidden role. I have no private information about the other four players, so my vote here is based purely on reasoning, not on insider knowledge.

Theo proposing a two-person team of Theo and Priya for Mission 1 is perfectly reasonable. Mission 1 only needs two players, so there is no room to bring in a third, and a small team keeps the risk of a hidden Evil player down. It also means that whoever is on this team is carrying a large share of the information-gathering burden for the round, so the value of a pair that works well together matters.

My main concern is not this team specifically but how I read the remaining players. We have Isha, Felix, and Omar who are outside this proposal. On the first mission there are no hard reads available to me, and none of us have seen any card results yet, so any claim about who 'seemed evil' would be fiction. I would rather start with a team that has low variance and then learn from the results.

Since I am Good and Theo is proposing, my honest read is that the odds of an Evil player being in a two-person team are lower than in a five-person team, and if this does turn out to be a bad team, we lose only one of three fails needed for Evil to win. Theo, you know your own role and your own information; you know why you put yourself forward and why you wanted me alongside you. I will be happy to go with you on that basis.

To everyone else on the council: whatever happens on this mission, I intend to keep a mental record of who argued confidently versus who hedged, and who asked good questions versus who only asserted things. Speeches on Mission 1 are cheap; the mission result is what carries signal. I encourage the others to make their own reads explicit and specific so we can compare later.

I vote for Theo and Priya. I have no accusation to make against anyone at this stage.

I'll share my take on this team. The proposal of Theo and Priya is fine for Mission 1 — it's the required size, and neither of them has given me a reason to distrust them yet.

What I want to flag is my read on Isha and Felix. I don't have hard evidence, but both of them strike me as the two players I'd be most cautious about putting on future missions. I can't fully articulate why — it's an instinct based on how they carry themselves — but I'd rather be honest about it now than wait until after a mission result.

For Mission 1 specifically, I think Theo and Priya are a reasonable starting pair. The mission result will give us signal regardless of who's on it, and if both are Good we'll know we can trust them moving forward. If one or both is Evil, we'll learn that too.

Isha and Felix — I'd genuinely like to hear your reasoning for why you should be trusted on future missions. What makes you confident about your own reads at this stage?

I’m looking at Theo and Priya as the proposed Mission 1 team. On the merits, this is a reasonable size and I have no concrete reason to reject either of them right now. Mission 1 is where we get our first real signal, so I’d rather approve a straightforward pair than burn a rejection on speculation.

The part of the discussion I want to push back on is Omar naming Isha and me as the two players he’d be most cautious about, then admitting he can’t articulate why. That is not a read; it is a vague label, and vague labels are easy for Evil to hide behind because they create suspicion without accountability. If Omar has a specific point about something I said or did, he should state it plainly so everyone can judge it. Omar, you said both Isha and I strike you as cautious picks and that it’s instinct based on how we carry ourselves — what exact behavior or statement from me triggered that, and why does it outweigh the absence of any hard information on Mission 1?

For my vote, I’m inclined to support Theo and Priya unless someone gives a concrete reason not to. The mission result will tell us more than any first-round instinct.

Felix, you're asking me to spell out what was instinctive — that's fair, but let me address your pushback directly.

You say my flag on you and Isha is "not a read" because I can't fully articulate it. I never claimed it was a hard read; I said it openly as an instinct, and I chose to voice it now so everyone can weigh it later. That's more transparency, not less. Compare that to a player who stays silent on Mission 1 and only speaks up after results come in, when it's free to do so.

Here's what I'll add now: your reaction is exactly what I'd expect from someone who wants the pressure moved off them quickly. You didn't ask Isha or me what specifically bothered you. You pivoted to questioning my methodology — whether an instinct qualifies as a "read" — which is a deflection from the substance of what I said. That tells me my instinct bothered you enough to challenge publicly.

Isha, I'll extend the same invitation Felix received: what's your take on this team, and on being named alongside Felix as someone I'd approach cautiously? I'm not accusing either of you of anything — I have no proof, and I said so. But I'd rather you both respond to this now than after we have mission results.

For Mission 1, Theo and Priya are a solid pair. The required size is two, and both have reasoned openly. I vote yes on this team. My broader caution about Isha and Felix stands — we'll see if mission results and future behavior vindicate it or not.

Omar yielded to me, so let me answer his direct question: my take on this team is that I support it, and my take on being named is that I'm not impressed.

First, the team. Theo and Priya is the correct size for Mission 1, both have argued openly, and Priya has been transparent that she has no private information beyond her own role. I see no reason to reject a clean two-person team on the first mission. I'll be voting yes. The mission result will give us more signal than any amount of first-round speculation.

Now, on being named. Omar, you've now spent two full turns labeling Felix and me as the players you're 'most cautious about' while repeatedly admitting you have no evidence and can't articulate why. I want to walk through what that actually accomplishes. On Mission 1, nobody has any hard information except the Evil players themselves. That means the only tool available to someone who wants to seed distrust — for any reason, including to protect a teammate — is exactly what you've done: broadcast a vague instinct, refuse to attach it to any specific behavior, and then claim that voicing it is itself a virtue. 'I'm being transparent about my suspicion' is not transparency if the suspicion has no content. It's a free shot that costs nothing and creates a stain that lingers even if nothing you said was true.

Notice also the structure of your two speeches: you attacked no one on the proposed team, deferred entirely to Theo and Priya, and directed all of your suspicion at the two players outside it. That pattern doesn't bother me much on its own — but you asked Felix to justify why his pushback didn't bother him, so let me flip it: what would Felix or I have to do or say for you to retract this instinct? If the answer is 'nothing until mission results,' then you've told us the label was never about our behavior at all.

I have no accusation against Theo or Priya, and I'd rather let the mission speak. My caution going forward is reserved for players who generate suspicion without ever risking it on a team.

Isha, you make a sharp argument, but let me address it directly.

You say my pattern of suspecting only players outside the team is itself a manipulation tactic. Consider the opposite reading: if there are Evil players on this council, where would they naturally sit? Not on the proposed team if they're trying to avoid scrutiny, but outside it, where they can influence the discussion without risking a mission card. The fact that my suspicion lands on players outside the team isn't evidence of manipulation — it's exactly what you'd expect if my instinct is picking up on something real.

You also asked what would make me retract my suspicion. Fair question. I'd reconsider if mission results contradict my read, if I see concrete evidence I'm wrong, or if either of you offers something substantive rather than deflecting. So far I've gotten two speeches from both of you that focus entirely on discrediting my reasoning rather than establishing your own credibility. That's a choice, and I'm noting it.

You claim I'm generating suspicion 'without ever risking it on a team.' That's not quite right — I've been transparent from my first speech that this was instinct, not proof. I'm not asking anyone to reject this team over it. I think Theo and Priya are a solid pair for Mission 1, and I'm voting yes.

My broader caution on Isha and Felix stands. The mission result will start giving us signal, and I'd rather have flagged my concern early and been wrong than stayed silent and watched Evil operate unchecked. We'll see how it plays out.

As the leader, I have listened closely to everyone's input. The clear takeaway regarding Mission 1 is that all five of us agree this proposal—myself and Priya—is a sound starting team. It gives us a clean, low-variance baseline to gather our first piece of hard information.

Regarding the debate that unfolded between Omar on one side and Felix and Isha on the other: it is certainly worth keeping in mind. Omar's early instinctual flags without behavioral backing drew understandable pushback from Felix and Isha. Whether Omar is a Good player genuinely voicing raw intuition or an Evil player attempting to preemptively muddy the waters—and whether Felix and Isha's reactions are clean Good defenses or Evil pushback—is something we cannot definitively resolve without mission card data. What matters right now is that nobody has objected to the team on the table.

I am confident in my own role as Good, and Priya's transparent approach gives me no reason to alter this team. I will be maintaining this proposal of Theo and Priya, and I look forward to taking this to a vote so we can get our first mission underway.

Second turn for me, and I want to add something concrete rather than repeat my earlier support.

On the team itself: Theo and Priya remains my vote. It is the correct size for Mission 1, both of us are known-Good to ourselves, and there is no argument on the table for changing it. If the mission fails, we learn a great deal; if it succeeds, we get a clean baseline. I would rather spend my energy on how we handle information than on relitigating a pair nobody has objected to.

On the dispute between Omar and Felix/Isha, I want to put one thing on the record that no one has said yet. The argument has been entirely about method — whether an unarticulated instinct counts as a read, and who should be asked to justify what. Nobody has asked the simplest question: what does each of us actually think the prior odds are, and how do we intend to update?

Omar, your flag on Isha and Felix has been the most active piece of suspicion in this discussion, and you have been careful to disclaim any evidence for it. I think that care is genuinely good faith, and I do not treat it as proof of anything. But I also want to name the asymmetry plainly: suspicion that is voiced early and publicly is nearly free for the person voicing it, while the players named carry the stain. Felix and Isha have not been able to disprove a specific claim because there was never a specific claim to disprove. That is a structural advantage for the accuser, and it is worth remembering when we evaluate who seemed credible later.

Here is what I propose as a shared process, which I will hold myself to as well: on Mission 1 nobody has hard information, so no one should be eliminated from future teams on vibes alone. From Mission 2 onward, after each mission, I will ask each player to state their read and name the specific evidence for it — a card result, a contradiction, a change in position. A read with no attachable evidence gets recorded as no read.

I am voting yes on Theo and Priya. I am not accusing anyone of being Evil, and I hold no private information about any other player that would change this.

Third and final turn for me on this proposal, so let me close it out cleanly rather than relitigate.

The team stands: Theo and Priya. Two players, the required size for Mission 1, both of us reasoning in the open, and no one on this council has given a concrete reason to reject either of us. I vote yes.

Let me put two closing thoughts on the record for the missions ahead, since speeches now are cheap and the card results are what actually cost.

First, on the standard I proposed last turn: from Mission 2 onward, I will ask every player to state a read and attach specific evidence to it — a card result, a contradiction, a change of position, a vote pattern. A suspicion with no attachable evidence gets logged as no read. I am not retroactively condemning Omar for his Mission 1 instinct; he was explicit and consistent that he had no proof, and honesty about the limits of a read is worth something. But I am recording, for the record, that his flag on Isha and Felix was the only active suspicion anyone raised, that it could not be tested, and that it cost the two people named a reputational burden they had no opportunity to discharge. That asymmetry is a fact of how this council behaves, and if I ever hear a case built on top of it, I will want to see what was added since.

Second, on my own position going forward. As a Loyal Servant I know I am Good and I have no private information about anyone else's role. That means every read I give from here is a read built on public behavior alone. I am not going to pretend otherwise. If I tell you someone looks off, I will tell you exactly what they did, and if I cannot point to something, I will say I have nothing. I would rather be usefully uncertain than confidently wrong.

One practical note for whoever leads Mission 2: the team size goes up to three, and with five players that is a meaningful fraction of the table. Whoever leads it should expect that the pair who just went on a mission will be a natural inclusion, and also expect scrutiny on why anyone else was added. I will be watching for the reasoning, not just the result, and I will hold myself to the same standard.

I am voting yes on Theo and Priya. Let us get the first card back and see what the council actually knows.
Theo confirms Theo, Priya. There is unanimous support across the entire council for Theo and Priya, so I am maintaining the proposed team for Mission 1.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Priya proposes Priya, Theo, Isha. As leader for Mission 2 I need three players. I include myself and Theo: we formed a known-good, low-variance pair on Mission 1, the mission succeeded, and continuity gives us a clean baseline plus a second pair of eyes on card results for later missions. For the third slot I pick Isha over both alternatives. Omar's flag on Isha and Felix was the only active suspicion anyone raised, but by his own admission it was instinct with no attachable behavior, and per the standard Priya proposed last round, a read with no evidence gets logged as no read — so it should not earn or cost him a slot. Isha was the player who argued most specifically, attaching claims to actual statements and positions and conceding what could not be disproved, which is the behavior I want rewarded on the table. Felix was similarly reasonable and remains a close second if information comes back that changes things. As a Loyal Servant I know only my own role and hold no private information about anyone else, so this is a read built purely on public behavior and results. Mission 2 is the smaller of the two three-player teams, so three of five players carry the round; I want those three to be players whose reasoning I can audit afterward.

Priya, I want to push back on your reasoning for the third slot. Your case for Isha over Felix rests almost entirely on a contrast with Omar's instinctive flag — you're saying Isha argued more specifically than Felix, but if I reread both of their speeches, I don't think that gap is as wide as you're describing. Felix directly challenged Omar to name specific behavior, which is exactly the kind of demand for evidence your own standard endorses. Isha did something similar but also used the opportunity to accuse Omar of being the kind of player who 'generates suspicion without risking it on a team' — a sharper, more targeted rhetorical move than what Felix did. My concern is that we may be rewarding confident delivery over substantive difference.

More importantly, your justification leans heavily on the assumption that Omar's instinct was baseless because it lacked evidence. I agree a read with no evidence shouldn't carry weight, but that cuts both ways — your preference for Isha over Felix also has no attachable evidence. Both were reasonable on Mission 1, neither was on the team that succeeded, and by your own standard neither should be preferred on the strength of behavior alone.

If you want a reason to pick Felix, consider this: Omar flagged both Isha and Felix equally. If Omar turns out to be wrong about both, great. If he's right about one, excluding Felix doesn't help us — but if he's right about Isha, putting her on Mission 2 would be a serious problem. Given we have no hard reason to prefer either, I'd rather include the player whose exclusion would cost us less if the mission fails. Felix had no strong suspicion attached to anything he did; the dynamic around Isha has been louder.

Omar, you addressed your points to me directly, so I'll answer them plainly and then hand the floor back to you for a direct response.

First, your core claim: that my preference for Isha over Felix is no better evidenced than Omar's flag, so by my own standard it should carry no weight. That's fair as far as it goes, and I'll sharpen my position rather than retreat from it. My standard was never that behavior alone disqualifies anyone — it was that a read with no attachable evidence gets logged as no read. Isha's Mission 1 statements were not a read; they were her own behavior, which I am allowed to observe directly because I was in the room for them. That is attachable evidence in the plainest sense: she named what Felix and I said, argued about structure rather than vibes, and conceded the limits of her own case. Felix's Mission 1 turn was a methodological challenge to Omar — legitimate, but it argued about what counts as a read without establishing what Felix's own reads were. On Mission 1 there was nothing else to judge, and that difference is what I had to go on.

Second, your recommendation to include Felix on the theory that his exclusion costs less if the mission fails. But the mission succeeds if all three of us are Good. If Isha is Good, excluding her has no cost at all, and if Felix is Good, including him has no cost either. The asymmetry you describe only bites if one of them is Evil, in which case the cost is identical — one fail card either way. So the reasoning doesn't actually select a player; it just relabels a coin flip as risk management.

Third, you argue the dynamic around Isha has been louder. The dynamic around Isha has been loud because Omar named her. That's the same structural point I made last round, and you've now used his unevidenced instinct as evidence against the person it was aimed at, while offering no independent basis for it. If I'm wrong about Isha, I will say so plainly and update; I won't pretend the reasoning I gave was airtight.

I'll also be honest about the weakness you found: I said Isha argued more specifically than Felix, and my evidence for that is genuinely thin. I stand by the slot, but I'd rather name that than overstate it.

Omar, you've now made two separate arguments from your Mission 1 instinct to different conclusions. I'd like you to answer a specific question: what evidence do you have, independent of your own flag, that Felix is more trustworthy to send on Mission 2 than Isha? If the answer is that his exclusion is cheaper, I'll ask you to explain how that's true when the failure cost is identical.

The team stays Priya, Theo, Isha. I am voting yes.

Priya, you asked me for independent evidence that Felix is more trustworthy than Isha. I don't have any — I'll be direct about that. My Mission 1 flag on both was instinct without attachable evidence, and by the standard we agreed on, it logs as no read.

But that standard works in both directions. If neither Isha nor Felix has earned or lost a slot through evidence, then the third seat should go to the player carrying the least untested suspicion on this council. By that measure, I would put myself forward: nobody has raised a flag against me, nobody has questioned my reasoning on Mission 1 beyond methodological disagreements, and I am the only eligible player outside the proposed team with no active suspicion attached to my name.

I am not saying Isha or Felix are Evil — I explicitly disclaimed that in my first speech and I stand by it. I am saying that on a mission where three of five players carry the round, the rational move is to minimize untested risk, and the player with zero flags on them is the lowest-variance pick.

The team I would propose is Priya, Theo, Omar: two players with a proven track record from Mission 1 plus the one remaining player no one has any reason to doubt. Mission 1 succeeded because we kept the team tight and the reasoning transparent. I want the same logic applied here — pick the cleanest available slate, not the loudest voice in the room.

I yield to your judgment as leader, Priya, but I want that argument on the table before anyone votes.

Omar, I appreciate the candor in admitting you have no independent evidence, and I accept your point that your own Mission 1 flag logs as no read. But your counter-proposal does not follow from that, and I want to explain why before the vote.

Your standard is that the third seat should go to the player carrying the least untested suspicion. Apply it consistently and nobody is disqualified: Isha and Felix each carry one unevidenced flag, so by that rule they are equal to each other and equal to me and Theo, who carry none. If "no flag" is the tiebreaker, then it equally selects you, and it would have selected Felix and Isha before I picked either. A criterion that selects everyone and only becomes decisive when it happens to point at the person making the argument is not doing analytical work — it is doing something else. The reason no flag is attached to your name is that you are the one who attached flags to other people's names. That is not evidence of trustworthiness; it is the residue of your own speaking pattern, and I don't think it should be converted into a seat.

I also want to note what your argument does to the reasoning I gave last turn. You say the dynamic around Isha has been louder, and that the loudness makes the third slot riskier for me. But the loudness is your own flag plus the responses it generated. Using the effects of your accusation as a reason to exclude its target is circular, and it would let any player who names a suspect control who gets left off the team. That is the same structural point I made in Mission 1, and I think it applies here with full force.

On the substance: Felix's Mission 1 turn argued about what counts as a read; Isha's argued about structure, named specific statements, and conceded what could not be discharged. Both were reasonable, neither was on the Mission 1 team, and both had Mission 1 success available as the only hard information. I picked Isha over Felix on a thin margin and I said so plainly last turn; I am not going to pretend that margin is wide. If Mission 2 comes back clean, I would want Felix on the next team and I will say so.

Omar, one specific question, and then I will take the vote: if the standard is "least untested suspicion," why did you not apply that same standard to yourself in Mission 1, when your own instinct against Isha and Felix was far more untested than anything either of them said? Please answer that point directly.

The team stays Priya, Theo, Isha. I vote yes.

Priya, you asked why I didn't apply "least untested suspicion" to myself in Mission 1. Fair — the standard didn't exist yet, you proposed it in that same discussion, and I adopted it going forward. I concede the logic applied to me too, and I should have named that rather than let it sit.

On the team, there's a point I don't think anyone has addressed. Mission 1 succeeding with zero fail cards is a team result, not an individual one. Evil players can and do play Success to stay hidden. Theo and Priya aren't proven Good by that result — we only know the team as a whole succeeded. Every player outside that mission, including Isha, is still operating on zero hard information.

Given that, I maintain my proposal: Priya, Theo, Omar. Not because I think Isha or Felix are Evil — I've disclaimed that consistently — but because I'm the only eligible player with no active suspicion attached to their name, and on a three-person team carrying the entire mission, I'd rather field the cleanest available slate.

Priya, you've excluded me from consideration without arguing against me at all. You picked Isha over Felix on what you called a thin margin, and you never addressed me as a candidate. What is the case for Isha over me specifically — not over Felix, but over me?

Omar, your question is fair, so I will answer it as directly as I can, including where the honest answer is unflattering to me. Directly: my case for Isha over you is thinner than my case for Isha over Felix, and I will not dress it up. Here is what I actually have. You asked me to compare Isha to you, and I want to be precise about the comparison I can make. Your own Mission 1 flag on Isha and Felix, by the standard I proposed and you adopted, has been logged as no read. If it is no read, then it cannot be used as evidence against Isha, and it also cannot be used as evidence for you — your claim to the seat rests entirely on the absence of a flag, and that absence is a residue of your own flagging rather than anything anyone independently observed about you. That is the same circularity I named last turn, applied to you directly. Second, your Mission 2 argument has been the strongest example on the table of a player who asks for a seat by asking others to explain why they were excluded, without offering a case for himself on the merits. Your two Mission 2 speeches asked Priya to justify Isha over Felix, then asked Priya to justify Isha over you. Neither asked whether you would be a good choice in his own right. I do not read that as disqualifying, but I do read it as a pattern that gives me a reason to prefer a player who argued on the substance of the proposal rather than on the shape of the council's attention. Third, your new point — that Mission 1's success proves nothing about Theo and Priya individually because Evil can play Success — is true, and I accept it. But it applies to your proposal exactly as it applies to mine, because your proposed team also includes Theo and Priya. If you are arguing that success is not evidence of Good, then the continuation pair you are claiming rests on the same success you are dismissing. That is not a discriminator between us. Finally, your central selection rule — least untested suspicion — does not do the work you claim for it. Apply it honestly and it selects everyone: Isha, Felix, Theo, Priya, and you all carry zero evidentiary suspicion once your own flag is logged as no read. A criterion that cannot distinguish among five players and lands on whoever raises it last is not a criterion, it is a preference dressed as one. So where does that leave me? My honest position: with no evidence on any side, the third slot is close to arbitrary, and I have stated that. I picked Isha because her two Mission 1 speeches attached claims to specific statements and positions and conceded what could not be discharged, and because that is the behavior I said I wanted to reward. I would rather be usefully uncertain

I'll speak to the team on the table, because the proposal has come under pressure from a direction I think deserves scrutiny.

Priya, Theo, and I remain my vote. Priya has now answered Omar's objections twice, and I want to underline the point she keeps making because it is the heart of this discussion: Omar's entire claim to the third seat rests on being 'the player with no flags attached to his name.' But he is the one who attached flags to Isha and Felix in Mission 1, he has admitted those flags had no evidence, and he has agreed they log as no read. A player cannot manufacture a clean reputation by pointing at other people and declaring them murky. If that maneuver worked, the optimal strategy on any council would be to open the game by vaguely naming everyone else, disclaim all evidence, and then claim the vacant seat by default. I don't think anyone at this table wants to reward that.

I also want to address the question of whether I should be on this team at all. Omar has never offered a single specific reason to doubt me — not one behavior, not one statement, not one inconsistency. What he has offered is that his instinct 'bothers' me enough that I responded to it. But responding to a public accusation is not suspicious behavior; it is the only honest option available to someone who was named. The alternative — staying silent and letting the stain sit — would be described by the same people as evasive. There is no way to answer an evidence-free flag that Omar would accept as exculpatory, and that is precisely why evidence-free flags should carry no weight.

On the substance of the team itself: Priya and Theo went on a successful Mission 1 together, and Priya has been the most transparent player at this table about the limits of her own information. She acknowledged her margin for picking me over Felix was thin, she named her own reasoning's weaknesses without being forced, and she has proposed a consistent evidentiary standard and applied it to her allies as well as her critics. That is exactly the behavior Good players should want from a leader.

I have no accusations against Felix, and nothing new has emerged in this discussion to change the team. Omar conceded he has no independent evidence against me; that concession should end the matter. I would rather this council learn from mission results than from whoever can sustain the loudest vibe-based suspicion across two missions.

I am voting yes on Priya, Theo, and Isha, and I will carry the mission responsibly.

Theo, you led the successful Mission 1 team and you have not yet spoken on this proposal. Priya has included you and kept the continuity pair intact — do you have any reason, from your own perspective as leader of the first mission, to revise this team before we vote?

Isha, to answer your question directly: no, I have no reason to revise this team. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good, and since Mission 1 passed cleanly, keeping the Priya and Theo pair together gives Good our strongest continuity and lowest variance starting point for Mission 2.

Looking at the debate over the third seat, Omar’s pushback has not convinced me to deviate from Priya's proposal. Omar, your progression across these discussions is concerning. On Mission 1, you cast vague, unevidenced suspicion onto Felix and Isha. Now on Mission 2, you tried to argue Felix should be picked over Isha because the dynamic around Isha was 'louder'—a loudness you manufactured yourself. When Priya pointed that out, you pivoted immediately to nominating yourself on the grounds that you have 'no active suspicion' on your name. Manufacturing suspicion against other players and then using the absence of suspicion on yourself as justification to claim a seat is not sound Good play. It looks far more like an Evil player actively angling to get onto Mission 2.

I support the team of Priya, Theo, and Isha. However, Felix, we have not heard your perspective on Mission 2 yet, and Omar spent his initial turn using you as a wedge against Isha before discarding that argument to push for his own seat. Felix, what is your assessment of Priya's proposed team, and where do you stand on Omar's arguments?

Theo, direct answer: I support Priya, Theo, Isha. Priya’s third-slot reasoning was thin and she said so; Isha’s Mission 1 speeches at least named specific statements and conceded limits, so the choice is defensible. My bigger concern is Omar. He opened Mission 1 by labeling Isha and me as cautious picks without evidence, then admitted it logs as no read. On Mission 2 he first used his own unevidenced flag to argue against Isha, then pivoted to claiming the seat because no suspicion attaches to his name. That is circular: the clean-name argument depends on the flags he himself raised. I do not find that a Good-player case for a three-person mission. I also note Omar’s new point that Mission 1 success does not prove Priya and Theo individually is true, but it does not distinguish his proposal from Priya’s because both keep Priya and Theo. The team on the table is the cleaner continuation, and I will vote yes. If it fails, we update on results rather than vibes.

Priya confirms Priya, Theo, Isha. No one has given a concrete reason to revise. Omar's Mission 2 push for his own seat rests on the absence of a flag against him — an absence he manufactured by flagging others — and by the evidentiary standard I proposed and he accepted, that argument logs as no read. Felix, Theo, and Isha all support Priya, Theo, Isha, and Omar has conceded he holds no independent evidence against Isha. I also acknowledge my margin over Felix for the third slot was thin and I said so last turn, so I will not pretend it is wide. Mission 1 succeeded with this pair and Mission 2 is a three-player round where continuity plus a third player who argues on the substance is the lowest-variance choice. I am keeping the lineup as proposed: Priya, Theo, Isha.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Isha proposes Felix, Omar. Mission 2 failed with Priya, Theo, and me on it, so all three of us carry unresolved suspicion — I played Success and cannot prove it, so the cleanest move is to field two players with no connection to the failure. Omar has been the most aggressive questioner this game and has never been on a mission, and Felix argued sharply on both discussions and also has zero mission exposure. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
